headline: Lost Forest of Giants Found in Taiwan's Mountains
meta_description: Scientists discovered Taiwan's hidden old-growth forests filled with giant Taiwania firs, including East Asia's tallest tree at 84.1 meters.
summary_short: Researchers found an 84.1-meter tree and hundreds of giants in Taiwan's remote mountains using LiDAR and citizen science—revealing one of Earth's richest carbon ecosyste…
body:
Since 2014, a team of professional climbers, ecologists, and remote sensing specialists has searched Taiwan's steep mountains for the island's most extraordinary inhabitants: giant trees that rise over 80 meters above the forest floor. In January 2023, their persistence paid off. After tracing a river for 20 kilometers and hiking steeply for two days, they discovered an 84.1-meter-tall Taiwania fir—now recognized as the tallest known tree in all of East Asia. The Indigenous Rukai people call these immense firs "the tree that hits the moon," a poetic name that feels almost literal when standing before specimens of this scale.

Finding individual giants proved less difficult than finding them all. Taiwan's steep, inaccessible terrain had protected old-growth forests from industrial logging that ravaged the island from 1912 to 1991. But searching among 950 million trees scattered across mountains and deep valleys required innovation. Researchers partnered with specialists at National Cheng Kung University to deploy LiDAR—an aircraft-based laser scanning system that builds precise 3D maps of terrain and tree height. The technology revealed a problem: automated software misidentified 93% of potential candidates, fooled by cliffs and elevation changes. The solution came from hundreds of Taiwanese citizens who, beginning in 2020, examined LiDAR images and eliminated false leads. By 2022, this collaboration had produced the "Taiwan Giant Tree Map," documenting 941 individual trees taller than 65 meters.

What emerged was not just a collection of individual records, but an undiscovered world. Researchers found dense "temples of giants"—places where dozens of enormous trees grow together—scattered across Taiwan's 36,000 square kilometers. These ancient forests rank among the planet's richest carbon-storing ecosystems, holding some of Earth's greatest natural carbon vaults. In protecting these hidden mountains, Taiwan has inadvertently preserved something precious: a living reminder of what old-growth forests can become when given time.
quick_facts: 84.1-meter Taiwania fir discovered in January 2023—tallest tree in East Asia
941 giant trees over 65 meters mapped across Taiwan's remote mountains
Citizen scientists eliminated 93% of false candidates in LiDAR data
Indigenous Rukai call these trees 'the tree that hits the moon'
Steep terrain protected old-growth forests from 1912–1991 logging era
